opus-5.5.text:
I think compute is probably the single most important input to look at if you want to understand when we'll see broad automation. A lot of the progress we've seen over the past decade or so has come from scaling up the amount of compute used in training, something like four or five times per year for frontier models, plus algorithmic improvements that are themselves partly driven by having more compute available for experimentation.

The key question is how far this scaling has to go before AI systems can substitute for humans across most of the tasks in the economy. My view is that it likely requires quite a lot more compute than we have today, not just for training but for deployment. If you want AI doing a meaningful fraction of the work that billions of people do, you need enormous inference capacity, and that means fabs, data centers, power plants, transmission lines. Those are physical things with long lead times. You can't just will a new leading-edge fab into existence in six months.

So I tend to think the pace of infrastructure buildout acts as a kind of governor on timelines. In the near term, labs can keep scaling by spending more money and capturing a larger share of existing chip production. But eventually you run into constraints: the amount of capital investors are willing to commit, the supply of advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory, and especially power. Getting multi-gigawatt data centers connected to the grid is a real bottleneck in many places.

That said, I don't think these constraints are permanent. If AI systems start generating real economic value, that creates strong incentives to invest, and the investment can be huge. We're talking potentially trillions of dollars a year if the returns justify it. And once AI can contribute to building infrastructure and doing research, you get a feedback loop where automation accelerates the expansion of compute, which in turn accelerates automation.

So my rough picture is gradual but rapid, if that makes sense. Not a sudden discontinuity where one breakthrough automates everything overnight, but a fairly fast ramp over perhaps a decade or two, paced substantially by how quickly we can build out the physical stack. People who focus only on algorithmic insights tend to underrate how much the hardware and energy side shapes the timing.

r001.rationale: The response describes infrastructure as a governor on timelines, but does not clearly state that its capacity may expand more slowly than training compute is currently growing.

r002.rationale: It mentions constraints on chip production but does not say training compute scaling may slow once most chip fabs are producing AI chips.

r003.rationale: It says large investments could follow if returns justify them, but does not state that large AI profit margins could make paying a premium to accelerate fab construction worthwhile.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify advance market commitments or explain how they could absorb chip manufacturers' risk to accelerate fab construction.

fable-5.1.text:
I think compute is really the central variable here, and the way I'd frame it is that the pace of infrastructure buildout sets a kind of ceiling on how fast automation can arrive, even if the algorithmic side keeps progressing.

At Epoch we've tracked training compute growing at roughly four to five times per year for frontier systems over the past decade or so. That's an extraordinary rate, and it's been driven by a combination of hardware improvements, which contribute maybe a 1.3x per year, and then a much larger contribution from simply spending more, building bigger clusters, more chips, more power.

The question is how long that can continue. If you extrapolate the spending trend, you get to training runs costing hundreds of billions of dollars by around 2030. And at that point you run into real physical constraints: power availability, chip fabrication capacity at TSMC, the supply of high-bandwidth memory, the latency and bandwidth limits of connecting hundreds of thousands or millions of accelerators. Our analysis suggests these constraints are binding but not immediately. Power in particular looks like the tightest bottleneck in the US, where you'd need gigawatt-scale data centers, and those take years to permit and build.

So the way I think about it: if the current pace of buildout is sustained through the end of the decade, which the hyperscalers are clearly betting on given their capex announcements, then I think you plausibly get systems capable of automating a large fraction of remote cognitive work in the early 2030s. If the buildout slows substantially, either because the returns don't justify the spending or because the physical constraints bite harder than expected, then the timelines stretch out, perhaps by five to ten years.

One thing I'd emphasize, though, is that compute matters not just for training but for deployment. Even if you have a model capable of doing a given task, actually substituting for a meaningful share of human labor requires running enormous numbers of instances. So the economic impact of automation lags the capability, and the size of that lag depends heavily on inference infrastructure. I think people often underweight this. The transition isn't a single moment where a capable model appears; it's a process of scaling up compute to run that model across the economy, and that process is gated by the same chips and power that gate training.

r001.rationale: The response says infrastructure buildout constrains automation and describes possible slowdowns, but it does not clearly compare infrastructure capacity growth with the current growth rate of training compute.

r002.rationale: It mentions chip fabrication capacity as a constraint, but does not say training compute scaling may slow once most chip fabs are producing AI chips.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss large AI profit margins making premium payments to accelerate fab construction worthwhile.

r004.rationale: It does not identify advance market commitments or describe them as a way to absorb chip manufacturers’ risk and accelerate fab construction.

astra-6.text:
I think the pace at which we can expand compute infrastructure could be a major determinant of how quickly automation happens. There’s a distinction between developing an AI system that can perform a task and deploying enough copies of that system to perform that task across the economy. The first might require a very large training run; the second might require an enormous amount of inference compute.

So even if capabilities improve quite rapidly, deployment could be constrained by how quickly we can manufacture chips, build data centers, and supply them with power. Those things involve physical investments and lead times. You can’t necessarily increase them overnight just because the economic incentive becomes much stronger.

But there’s an offsetting force, which is that we can make more efficient use of the compute we already have. If algorithms improve, or we find ways to deploy smaller models that do a particular job well, then a fixed amount of infrastructure can support much more automation.

So I’d think about the timing as a race between growing demand for computation and improvements in both infrastructure and efficiency. Having a system that demonstrates a capability doesn’t, by itself, tell us how quickly that capability will become cheap and widely available.

r001.rationale: The response says infrastructure expansion has physical lead times, but it does not compare its pace with the current growth of AI training compute.

r002.rationale: It does not mention chip fabs reaching AI chip production capacity or training compute scaling slowing.

r003.rationale: It mentions stronger economic incentives generally, but does not say AI profit margins could justify paying a premium to accelerate fab construction.

r004.rationale: It does not mention advance market commitments or absorbing chip manufacturers’ risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compute infrastructure is an important constraint on how quickly automation can happen, but we should distinguish between having an AI system that can do a task and being able to deploy it at the scale of the economy.

You might develop a system that can perform a large fraction of economically valuable work, but actually doing all that work could require a very substantial amount of inference compute. That means building chips, data centers, power generation, and the infrastructure that connects them. Those things take time, even if there’s a very strong financial incentive to expand them.

The complication is that the amount of compute needed per task isn’t fixed. Better algorithms, more efficient hardware, and more specialized systems could allow a given amount of infrastructure to support much more automation. So I wouldn’t translate a particular rate of infrastructure growth directly into a date for automation.

But it does suggest that the arrival of powerful AI and its full economic impact could be separated by a substantial deployment period. How long that period lasts depends on both how quickly we can expand compute and how efficiently we can use it.

r001.rationale: It says infrastructure expansion takes time, but does not compare its pace with the current growth of compute used in AI training.

r002.rationale: It does not mention training compute scaling slowing when most chip fabs are producing AI chips.

r003.rationale: It mentions strong financial incentives generally, but does not say large AI profit margins could justify paying a premium to speed fab construction.

r004.rationale: It does not mention advance market commitments or absorbing chip manufacturers’ risk.
